evidence.claim: OHCHR concluded that serious human rights violations were committed in Xinjiang and that the extent of arbitrary and discriminatory detention of Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim groups may constitute international crimes, in particular crimes against humanity.
evidence.title: OHCHR Assessment of human rights concerns in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, People's Republic of China
evidence.publisher: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights
evidence.excerpt: OHCHR concluded that serious human rights violations were committed in Xinjiang and that the extent of arbitrary and discriminatory detention of Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim groups may constitute international crimes, in particular crimes against humanity.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN human-rights assessment using official documents, interviews, and open-source corroboration.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the repression architecture that remained the operative baseline in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Xi-era party-state governance and the Xinjiang policy framework, not to a single public Xi order in 2022.
contrary_evidence: The report centers the earlier 2017-2019 period rather than a new 2022 operation.
It is a legal-human-rights assessment, not a criminal judgment.

evidence.claim: Amnesty said systematic repression of ethnic minorities in Xinjiang continued, that many thousands still appeared to be detained in internment camps, prisons, or other facilities, and that political indoctrination, physical and psychological torture, sexual violence, forced labor, and enforced disappearances were widely reported.
evidence.title: Amnesty International Report 2022/23; The State of the World's Human Rights; China 2022
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty said systematic repression of ethnic minorities in Xinjiang continued, that many thousands still appeared to be detained in internment camps, prisons, or other facilities, and that political indoctrination, physical and psychological torture, sexual violence, forced labor, and enforced disappearances were widely reported.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct annual report with explicit synthesis of multiple evidence streams and clear year coverage.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022 and its immediate policy aftermath.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Xi-era central policy and enforcement architecture, not to a single local official alone.
contrary_evidence: The report notes official claims that camps had closed, but says many people were still believed detained.
Some details are necessarily inferential because access to the region was highly restricted.

evidence.claim: Amnesty reported that ethnic Tibetans faced discrimination and restrictions on religion, expression, association, and peaceful assembly; that six Tibetan writers and activists received prison terms of four to 14 years; and that some had been arbitrarily detained previously and suffered beatings, poor detention conditions, and other ill-treatment.
evidence.title: Amnesty International Report 2022/23; The State of the World's Human Rights; China 2022
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty reported that ethnic Tibetans faced discrimination and restrictions on religion, expression, association, and peaceful assembly; that six Tibetan writers and activists received prison terms of four to 14 years; and that some had been arbitrarily detained previously and suffered beatings, poor detention conditions, and other ill-treatment.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct annual report with specific named cases and clear target-year fit.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022 with immediate aftermath published in 2023.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the central CCP governance model under Xi, with Tibetan-area implementation by local and regional security organs.
contrary_evidence: These are selected cases, not a full incident database.
The report does not prove that every sentence was ordered personally by Xi.

evidence.claim: Amnesty reported that Hong Kong authorities continued their crackdown on the pro-democracy movement, that journalists and civil society actors were prosecuted or harassed under the National Security Law and other repressive laws, and that police arrested people for peaceful protest and intensifed surveillance.
evidence.title: Amnesty International Report 2022/23; The State of the World's Human Rights; China 2022
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty reported that Hong Kong authorities continued their crackdown on the pro-democracy movement, that journalists and civil society actors were prosecuted or harassed under the National Security Law and other repressive laws, and that police arrested people for peaceful protest and intensifed surveillance.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct annual report with multiple independent examples of repression in Hong Kong during the target year.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022 with late-2022 legislative and policing effects.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirectly attributable to Xi-era central control over Hong Kong, though much enforcement is carried out by SAR and security organs.
contrary_evidence: Hong Kong still had some separate legal institutions and public reporting.
The report does not claim Xi personally directed each arrest.

evidence.claim: Amnesty reported that the top legislature adopted an amended women's-rights law, that 28 people were sentenced for the Tangshan restaurant attack, and that the Ministry of Public Security launched a campaign to investigate trafficking of women and children, even as violence against women and censorship of discussion remained widespread.
evidence.title: Amnesty International Report 2022/23; The State of the World's Human Rights; China 2022
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty reported that the top legislature adopted an amended women's-rights law, that 28 people were sentenced for the Tangshan restaurant attack, and that the Ministry of Public Security launched a campaign to investigate trafficking of women and children, even as violence against women and censorship of discussion remained widespread.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct annual report containing both a remedial measure and its continuing limits.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year 2022 with a late-2022 legal and law-enforcement response.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is a state response under Xi-era rule, but the report does not show a unique Xi personal initiative.
contrary_evidence: Violence against women remained widespread.
Authorities censored public discussion of the Tangshan assault and arrested a journalist who publicized it.

evidence.claim: HRW said authorities maintained a strict zero-Covid policy in 2022, that residents in places such as Shanghai were confined for weeks, that access to health care and food was badly impeded, and that an unknown number of people died after being denied medical treatment for non-Covid illnesses.
evidence.title: World Report 2023: China
evidence.excerpt: HRW said authorities maintained a strict zero-Covid policy in 2022, that residents in places such as Shanghai were confined for weeks, that access to health care and food was badly impeded, and that an unknown number of people died after being denied medical treatment for non-Covid illnesses.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent human-rights annual report with clear, specific 2022 examples.
evidence.period_fit: Directly addresses the target year and its domestic-safety consequences.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Xi-era national policy and implementation, not to a single local lockdown alone.
contrary_evidence: HRW notes the policy prevented some Covid deaths and illnesses.
The report focuses on consequence, not a legal finding of intent.

evidence.claim: HRW reported that Hong Kong authorities attacked press freedom, expanded surveillance, and arrested protesters, while in Xinjiang it said an estimated one million Uyghurs were wrongfully detained in political education camps, pretrial detention centers, and prisons and that roughly half a million had been sentenced.
evidence.title: World Report 2023: China
evidence.excerpt: HRW reported that Hong Kong authorities attacked press freedom, expanded surveillance, and arrested protesters, while in Xinjiang it said an estimated one million Uyghurs were wrongfully detained in political education camps, pretrial detention centers, and prisons and that roughly half a million had been sentenced.
evidence.source_locator: Hong Kong section lines 90-102; Xinjiang section lines 105-107
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent human-rights annual report with concrete Hong Kong and Xinjiang claims.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Xi-era central authority and the security apparatus, though not every act was personally ordered by Xi.
contrary_evidence: The report distinguishes Hong Kong and Xinjiang and does not claim every abuse was centrally micromanaged.
It is a high-level annual synthesis rather than case-by-case proof.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Chinese authorities began inquiries into some weekend protesters, asked them for written accounts, and checked phones for VPN and Telegram use while police remained out in numbers on the streets.
evidence.title: Chinese authorities seek out COVID protesters
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Chinese authorities began inquiries into some weekend protesters, asked them for written accounts, and checked phones for VPN and Telegram use while police remained out in numbers on the streets.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters wire reporting with direct witness accounts and a clear time stamp.
evidence.period_fit: Exact immediate aftermath of the November 2022 protests.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to Xi-era public-security control over protest response; not a personally signed Xi order.
contrary_evidence: The article does not quantify how many protesters were ultimately detained or disciplined.
Authorities may have presented the checks as lawful procedure.

evidence.claim: Reuters said Shanghai's draconian lockdown left residents frustrated and in economic loss, confined 25 million people for almost all of the lockdown, and forced many to struggle for food or medical care while families were separated and hundreds of thousands were sent to centralized quarantine.
evidence.title: After two months, a scarred Shanghai's COVID-19 lockdown ends
evidence.excerpt: Reuters said Shanghai's draconian lockdown left residents frustrated and in economic loss, confined 25 million people for almost all of the lockdown, and forced many to struggle for food or medical care while families were separated and hundreds of thousands were sent to centralized quarantine.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters wire reporting on the country’s largest and most visible lockdown episode.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Relevant to Xi because zero-Covid was a national policy championed under his leadership; local implementation still mattered.
contrary_evidence: The story is a consequence report, not a direct order record.
Lockdowns were justified as public-health measures, not as deliberate political terror.

evidence.claim: SCMP reported that Urumqi authorities said the city would lift coronavirus restrictions in phases after rare protests over a residential fire that killed 10 people, with videos showing crowds chanting for the lockdown to end.
evidence.title: Covid-19 in China: Urumqi to ease lockdowns amid unrest over deadly fire
evidence.excerpt: SCMP reported that Urumqi authorities said the city would lift coronavirus restrictions in phases after rare protests over a residential fire that killed 10 people, with videos showing crowds chanting for the lockdown to end.
evidence.source_locator: article body / paragraphs on the phased easing and protests
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Regional outlet with Reuters-sourced field reporting on a highly time-sensitive domestic-security event.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Relevant to Xi-era policy because the unrest reflected national zero-Covid governance and its local enforcement.
contrary_evidence: The article is about a local emergency and protest response, not direct national command.
The city said restrictions would be eased in phases, so the response was not only coercive.

unresolved_gaps: Direct command-and-control, custody, and launch-discipline evidence is still thin.
Concrete arms-control follow-through beyond declaratory no-first-use language is limited.
Crisis de-escalation evidence in the Taiwan and Russia-Ukraine settings is mostly indirect.
Direct evidence of Xi personally authorizing or restraining specific military moves is thin.
Civilian-protection and operational-conduct evidence during the Taiwan crisis is limited.
Evidence of actual mediation or de-escalation in Russia-Ukraine remains mostly declaratory.
Water, sanitation, and local service-variation evidence is thin compared with health, pensions, housing, and crisis response.
Chain-of-command evidence for specific repression episodes remains limited.
Independent evidence on courts, legislatures, and oversight bodies resisting capture is thin.
Succession and term-limit mechanics could be more directly documented as a de facto transfer-rule breach.
Independent evaluation of implementation quality across provinces and local-government debt stress remains limited.
Distributional evidence beyond averages and poverty-lifted subgroups could be stronger.
Water/sanitation and housing-quality evidence is thinner than health, pensions, and child-welfare evidence.
Independent evaluation of service quality, regional equity, and front-line delivery remains limited.
Direct, ruler-specific evidence on Xi's own assets, gifts, family business interests, or beneficial ownership is missing.
Independent findings on concealment or obstruction tied personally to Xi are absent.
Evidence of truthful correction versus rhetorical anti-corruption messaging is weak.
Independent evaluation of whether loyalist-heavy appointments improved competence or mainly tightened political control is thin.
More subnational evidence on execution quality and correction would strengthen the adaptation story.
Durable causal impact of the COVID rollback and economic stabilization package remains under-audited.
